articles.title: How the credit-reporting system actually works
articles.body:
Credit reporting companies — also called credit bureaus or consumer reporting agencies — are private businesses that compile and sell credit reports. They collect account information from lenders, credit card companies, collection agencies, and public records. Specialty bureaus collect even more, including employment and tenant history.

No one asks your permission. A company does not need your consent to report your account history to the bureaus. The federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) regulates what gets reported and who may see it — it does not ask whether you agreed to be tracked. Written consent is the narrow exception, not the rule: the FCRA requires your written authorization only in a few situations, like an employer pulling your report before hiring you (15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(2)(A)). Reporting is also voluntary on the other side — “Creditors are not required to report information to the credit reporting companies,” the CFPB says. They choose to. The system runs on decisions made about you, by companies you did not pick, under rules you never signed.

The same companies that supply the data are also its biggest buyers. The CFPB’s official overview of the industry found that most furnishers of account data to the nationwide bureaus are also large users of credit reports — they send information about you in, and they purchase information about you out. The bureaus are paid by the companies that use the data. You are the subject of the data, not the customer.

And when the data is wrong, the correction burden lands on you. Every repair duty in the FCRA is switched on by the consumer. Nothing in the law makes a bureau or a furnisher start a fix on its own. Someone else’s mistake becomes your letters, your postage, your waiting — unless and until you put it on the record.

The duties the law does impose are real — they just start with you. Once you notify a credit bureau of a dispute, it must “conduct a reasonable reinvestigation” free of charge and finish within 30 days (15 U.S.C. § 1681i(a)(1)(A)). Within five business days it must hand the company that furnished the item “all relevant information regarding the dispute” (§ 1681i(a)(2)(A)). And it must “review and consider all relevant information submitted by the consumer” (§ 1681i(a)(4)) — which is why what you send matters.

The furnisher then answers under its own deadline. It must conduct an investigation, review what the bureau forwarded, report the results back, and — if the information turns out incomplete or inaccurate — tell every other nationwide bureau too, all before that same 30-day window closes (15 U.S.C. § 1681s-2(b)(1)–(2)). Around those duties sit standing rules: a furnisher may not report information it “knows or has reasonable cause to believe” is inaccurate (§ 1681s-2(a)(1)(A)); it must promptly correct and update information it learns is wrong (§ 1681s-2(a)(2)); and once you dispute, it cannot keep reporting the item without noting the dispute (§ 1681s-2(a)(3)). You can also dispute directly to the furnisher at the address it specifies for disputes — the same investigation duties and the same deadline apply (§ 1681s-2(a)(8)(D)–(E)).

If the item cannot be verified or turns out wrong, the bureau must promptly delete or correct it (§ 1681i(a)(5)(A)). Deleted information cannot quietly come back: it may be reinserted only if the furnisher “certifies that the information is complete and accurate” (§ 1681i(a)(5)(B)(i)).

The remedies behind those duties are stronger than most people expect. If a bureau or furnisher is negligent, it owes your actual damages plus “the costs of the action together with reasonable attorney’s fees as determined by the court” (15 U.S.C. § 1681o(a)). If the failure was willful, the consumer can recover actual damages or statutory damages of “not less than $100 and not more than $1,000” even without showing a specific dollar harm, plus “such amount of punitive damages as the court may allow,” plus fees (§ 1681n(a)). The fee-shifting is deliberate design: it is what makes these cases possible for people who could never pay a lawyer by the hour.

When the furnisher is a debt collector — including the collectors a landlord hands an alleged balance to — a second law stacks on top. The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bars false representations about “the character, amount, or legal status of any debt” (15 U.S.C. § 1692e(2)(A)), bars collecting “any amount” not “expressly authorized by the agreement creating the debt or permitted by law” (§ 1692f(1)), and specifically bars “communicating… credit information which is known or which should be known to be false, including the failure to communicate that a disputed debt is disputed” (§ 1692e(8)). The remedy: actual damages, up to $1,000 more in statutory damages per person, and attorney’s fees (§ 1692k(a)).

Two clocks run at once. On the mark itself: most collection accounts must come off the report after seven years, counted from 180 days after the delinquency that started it all (15 U.S.C. § 1681c(a)(4), (c)(1)). On your remedies: an FCRA action must be brought within the earlier of two years after you discover the violation or five years after it happens (§ 1681p); FDCPA claims close in one year (§ 1692k(d)). Dates on the record are not bookkeeping. They are deadlines.

Here is why the order of the paper trail matters — analysis, not law. A written dispute to the bureau starts the 30-day clock and forces the bureau to hand the furnisher your documentation within five days. What the furnisher does next — correct it, verify it anyway, or stay silent — is now a decision made on the record, against a deadline, with your papers in its hands. That sequence is the difference between “the furnisher made a mistake” and “the furnisher was told, investigated, and reported it anyway.” The first reads as negligence. The second is the factual shape of willfulness — and willfulness is where statutory and punitive damages live. The CFPB itself tells consumers to send furnisher disputes in writing, by certified mail. The record is not preparation for leverage. The record is the leverage.

Minnesota adds its own layer. The state has its own consumer-reporting statute (Minn. Stat. ch. 13C) with its own definitions and duties, and it licenses collection agencies — including “debt buyers,” businesses “engaged in the purchase of any charged-off account, bill, or other indebtedness for collection purposes” (Minn. Stat. § 332.31, subds. 3, 8). A collector furnishing a tradeline while unlicensed raises questions worth asking.

For tenants this is not abstract. The CFPB lists landlords among the furnishers. An inflated move-out balance or a disputed charge can sit in a file and surface on the next rental application — through a regular credit report or a specialty tenant-history report. The same discipline that protects a tenancy — a clear, dated record — is the discipline this body of law was built to reward.

One next step: pull all three of your reports at AnnualCreditReport.com — the only website federally authorized to deliver the reports the law entitles you to, and free once a week at each bureau under a program the FTC says is now permanent. Look for landlord and collector tradelines. If something is wrong, dispute it in writing to the bureau and the furnisher, send it by certified mail, and keep every receipt and response with dates attached.

This is general educational information, not legal advice. For a specific situation, talk to a licensed attorney or your local legal aid society — and note that the fee-shifting described above is exactly why consumer attorneys can take these cases.
